## Overview

This part encodes residues 15 to 23 of BoPep4, a 23-residue plant elicitor peptide from broccoli (*Brassica oleracea* var. *italica*), with its native start and stop codons removed so that it can be fused to a signal peptide and a tag.

BoPep4 acts as a peptide hormone: it binds the plant PEPR receptor and raises defence signalling and salt tolerance. This construct keeps only the conserved C-terminal core, the part of the peptide that makes contact with the receptor, and removes the N-terminal residues entirely.

## Why this truncation

The full-length peptide and a ladder of N-terminal truncations were compared in molecular dynamics, scoring how reliably the Asn23 clamp with the receptor is held across a trajectory. The ladder is not monotonic. Full length, 7–23 and 15–23 all hold the clamp above 98% of frames, while the intermediate 9–23 construct falls to 77.1% clamp integrity and 46.9% bidentate occupancy. Shortening the peptide is therefore not what costs the contact; the loss at 9–23 comes from removing the Lys7 anchor while leaving a flexible N-terminal tail behind, and cutting further back to 15–23 removes that tail and restores the clamp.

This part is the short end of that ladder, carried as a candidate for the smallest construct that still engages the receptor.

## About

* Biosafety level: S1
* Target organism: *Bacillus subtilis* (WB800)
* Main purpose of use: a minimal BoPep4 core for secretion as a plant elicitor
* Potential application: raising plant defence signalling and salt tolerance

steps.label: Create design
steps.text:
## Overview

This Protectant Module constitutively expresses a truncated BoPep4 peptide and allows its secretion and detection to be assessed. It is a composite transcription unit with four elements, in this order:

* **Pveg** ([BBa\_K143012](https://registry.igem.org/parts/bba-k143012)): a constitutive *Bacillus subtilis* promoter that drives continuous transcription without induction.
* **EEBD-RBS0** ([BBa\_26V6CPEV](https://registry.igem.org/parts/bba-26v6cpev)): the *E. coli* expression blocking device followed by the ribosome binding site RBS0.
* **SamyQ-BoPep4 (9–23)-Histag**: the alpha-amylase signal peptide SamyQ fused to residues 9 to 23 of BoPep4, with a C-terminal 6x Histag for detection and purification.
* **B0015** ([BBa\_B0015](https://registry.igem.org/parts/bba-b0015)): a double terminator that prevents read-through into anything downstream.

## Why this truncation

In the molecular dynamics comparison of N-terminal truncations, the 9–23 construct is the one rung of the ladder that loses the receptor contact: clamp integrity falls to 77.1% and bidentate occupancy to 46.9%, where full length, 7–23 and 15–23 all stay above 98%. Under protonation at pH 5.5 the same construct drops bidentate occupancy to 6.9%, the only run in the set to fail its acceptance gate — neither the truncation nor the protonation does that alone, only the two together.

This cassette was built to carry that construct into the wet lab so the prediction could be tested rather than assumed.

## About

* Biosafety level: S1
* Target organism: *Bacillus subtilis* (WB800)
* Main purpose of use: constitutive expression and secretion of a truncated BoPep4
* Potential application: raising plant defence signalling and salt tolerance

BBa_26BDO8AQ.title: Pveg-RBS0-ccaR-B0015

BoPEP4.legend: **Figure 1 | BoPEP4 (1–23) bound in the PEPR1 leucine-rich-repeat groove.** The modelled complex of full-length BoPEP4 (orange, all atoms) against the 710-residue *Arabidopsis thaliana* PEPR1 ectodomain (green, Cα trace), taken from the first frame of a 30 ns all-atom molecular dynamics run in explicit solvent. The peptide lies extended along the inner face of the LRR solenoid; it does not fold into it. The dashed line marks the Asn23 to Arg487 contact that anchors the C terminus, 2.72 Å in this frame. Starting pose from HADDOCK 2.5 docking onto the AtPep1–PEPR1 crystal structure (PDB 5GR8); run R1_BoPep4_WT_PEPR1.

**Figure 2 | The binding groove, coloured by side-chain class.** Solvent-excluded surface of the 316 receptor residues lining the peptide-binding groove, computed with a 1.4 Å probe and coloured basic (blue), acidic (red), polar (teal) and apolar (grey). The groove is acidic along the stretch the peptide's lysines and arginines occupy, which is the electrostatic complementarity the design relies on. Surface points in front of the peptide are faded so the far wall of the groove stays readable. Run R1_BoPep4_WT_PEPR1.

**Figure 3 | The contact footprint over 30 nanoseconds.** The same receptor surface, shaded instead by the share of the 1,500 recorded frames in which each surface point lies within 4 Å of the peptide. Green marks surface the peptide holds; pale grey marks surface it never touches. The footprint is continuous along the groove, and it stops at the C-terminal pocket. Run R1_BoPep4_WT_PEPR1.

**Figure 4 | The C-terminal clamp of wild-type BoPEP4.** Close view of the C-terminal anchor, with the four receptor residues that close around Asn23 named: Arg487, Asn465, Asp441 and Ile443 (amber sticks, published numbering). Asn23 and its free carboxylate sit in the pocket; the dashed line is the Asn23 to Arg487 distance in this frame. This clamp held in 100.0% of frames in this run, which is the structural reason the C terminus was ruled off-limits for tagging. Run R1_BoPep4_WT_PEPR1.

**Figure 5 | BoPEP4 (9–23), the ordered construct, in the same groove.** The manufacturing candidate, fifteen residues against the wild type's twenty-three, modelled and simulated on the identical protocol. The anchor end is unchanged; what is gone is the N-terminal GILIGSKK segment and with it the Lys7 salt bridge that pins the 9–14 stretch. Against full length this construct carries 33% less mass (1,612.73 Da against 2,409.74 Da), one trypsin-type cut site instead of three, and half the positive charge. Run R1_BoPep4_9-23_PEPR1.

**Figure 6 | The same clamp under the 9–23 truncation.** The clamp view of Figure 4 repeated for the ordered construct. The four clamp residues are in place, but over the trajectory the clamp holds in only 77.1% of frames against 100.0% for wild type, and the bidentate Arg487 salt bridge beneath it in 46.9% against 100.0%. Removing an anchor without removing the segment it anchors is what costs the clamp here; the shorter 15–23 construct, which removes both, holds it in 99.9% of frames. Run R1_BoPep4_9-23_PEPR1.

**Figure 7 | BoPEP4 (7–23), the alternative cut.** The seventeen-residue construct, which keeps the Lys7 anchor that the 9–23 cut removes. Clamp integrity 98.5%, bidentate occupancy 87.7%: on the structural measures it is the steadier of the two cuts in this region, and the 9–23 construct was chosen over it on manufacturing grounds, not on binding. Run R1_BoPep4_7-23_PEPR1.

**Figure 8 | BoPEP4 (15–23), the conserved core alone.** Nine residues, the invariant Ser15 to Asn23 stretch, simulated as a control on whether length alone drives the loss seen at 9–23. It does not: this shorter construct holds the clamp in 99.9% of frames. Run R1_BoPep4_15-23_PEPR1.

**Figure 9 | BoPEP4 with a C-terminal His₆ tag.** The tagged construct, which appends six histidines past Asn23 and so replaces the free C-terminal carboxylate with an amide. The peptide stays in the groove and the backbone is the steadiest in the set, but the charged interaction at the anchor is gone: bidentate Arg487 occupancy falls to 2.4% from 100.0%. This run is the reason the purification tag was moved to the N terminus for every BoPEP4 construct ordered after 16 August. Run R1_BoPep4_WT_Chis_PEPR1.

**Figure 10 | AtPep1 (7–23) in PEPR1: the benchmark the protocol was checked on.** The published ligand of this receptor, simulated under the identical protocol as a positive control before any BoPEP4 result was accepted. All four hydrogen bonds reported in the crystal structure are reproduced (Table 2), which is what licenses reading the BoPEP4 runs at all. Reference run, batch 2026-08-20.

**Figure 11 | Wild-type BoPEP4 with all three histidines protonated, pH 5.5.** The same complex under the protonation state expected on a leaf surface rather than at neutral pH. Protonation recovers the Glu12 to His227 contact from 0.8% to 99.9% of frames and leaves the clamp at 100.0%: on full-length peptide, leaf pH helps. Run R1_BoPep4_WT_PEPR1_lowpH.

**Figure 12 | BoPEP4 (9–23) at pH 5.5, the only run in the set to fail its acceptance gate.** The same protonation applied to the ordered construct, which drops clamp integrity to 19.3% and bidentate occupancy to 6.9%. Neither the truncation alone nor the protonation alone does this; the combination does. This is an open structural risk against the construct that was ordered, and it is stated as one. Run R1_BoPep4_9-23_PEPR1_lowpH.

**Figure 13 | The anchor belt along the docked complex.** Ribbon rendering of the docked BoPEP4–PEPR1 model (peptide orange, receptor grey) with the basic side chains at positions 7, 9 and 18 reaching onto receptor carboxylates, distances labelled in ångström at 2.6 to 3.0 Å. Nothing on the peptide is buried before position 7; from there the belt runs the length of the concave face of the solenoid, and the C-terminal clamp of Figure 4 closes the end of it. Rendered from a docked model carrying Arg at position 18 rather than the wild-type Lys; the belt architecture is the same in every complex in the panel. Receptor residues are in that model's own numbering.

**Figure 14 | The Asn23 pocket in the docked model.** Surface rendering of the C-terminal pocket, showing that Asn23 sits inside the receptor rather than on the face of the interface, with its free α-carboxylate salt-bridging Arg487 at 2.40 Å in the crystal structure. There is no room for a residue 24 without the peptide leaving the pocket, which is the structural argument against a C-terminal tag. Read with Figure 4, which measures the same pocket over a trajectory instead of in one pose. ### Graphs of simulation and docking results

**Figure 15 | Both chains settle inside the acceptance window.** Backbone RMSD from the starting structure over 30 ns for the receptor Cα atoms (green) and the peptide backbone (orange), 1,500 frames at 20 ps. Dashed lines mark the acceptance thresholds set before the run: 3.0 Å for the receptor, 4.0 Å for the peptide. Neither trace crosses its threshold, so the trajectory is read as equilibrated, not drifting. Run R1_BoPep4_WT_PEPR1.

**Figure 16 | The four crystal contacts, held across the trajectory.** Heavy-atom distance over time for each of the four hydrogen bonds reported for the AtPep1–PEPR1 complex in PDB 5GR8, measured here in the BoPEP4 simulation. The solid line in each panel is the crystallographic distance, the dashed line the 1.5 Å tolerance the acceptance test allows. Occupancy and mean distance are printed per panel. Run R1_BoPep4_WT_PEPR1.

**Figure 17 | Contact occupancy and fluctuation, residue by residue.** For each of the 23 residues of wild-type BoPEP4: bars give the share of frames within 4 Å of the receptor, coloured by occupancy band, and the line gives Cα fluctuation (RMSF). Across residues 1 to 6 occupancy is uneven, from 16% at Gly5 to 99% at Ile2, and fluctuation stays above 1.7 Å throughout; from Glu12 onward fluctuation drops to between 0.72 and 1.01 Å at every position but Lys18, which sits at 1.39 Å, and occupancy is at or near 100% everywhere except Pro19 at 52%. Arg9 is on the boundary: 100% occupancy at a 1.32 Å fluctuation. Note that this is a 4 Å proximity measure over a trajectory, which is not the same as the buried-surface measure used in the docking interface map, where residues 1 to 6 bury no area at all. Run R1_BoPep4_WT_PEPR1.

**Figure 18 | The C-terminal clamp across the eight peptide-bearing runs.** Two measures of the same anchor for every construct simulated: clamp integrity (green), the strict measure used throughout the Protein Design pages, and the bidentate Arg487 salt bridge beneath it, resolved to atoms (amber). The dashed line is the project's 60% acceptance floor. The two measures agree everywhere except on the His₆-tagged construct, where clamp integrity reads 99.7% and the atom-resolved salt bridge reads 2.4%. A third, more tolerant clamp measure is used by the acceptance gate itself and is reported separately in Table 5.

**Figure 19 | Where the interface stops tolerating an N-terminal cut.** HADDOCK 2.5 water-refined score for seventeen successive N-terminal truncations of BoPEP4, each re-docked on the identical protocol, against PEPR1 (green) and PEPR2 (slate). Scores are flat for the first seven cuts and climb steadily thereafter. Lower binds better; the axis is inverted so that better binding is higher.

**Figure 20 | The same ladder scored by AlphaFold3.** Interface confidence (ipTM, upper panel) and interface predicted aligned error (lower panel) for each rung against both receptors. Confidence rises slightly as the disordered N terminus is removed, then collapses between 13–23 and 14–23. Our docking places the binding cliff at 9–23 and AlphaFold3 places it at 14–23; the project states the cliff as a range, 9 to 14, and names both methods instead of picking one.

**Figure 21 | What the docking score does not predict.** Pooled HADDOCK score against published half-maximal concentration for sixteen equal-length AtPep1 analogues from Pearce et al. 2008. The three analogues with measured loss of activity (red) sit in the middle of the docking ranking, not at the bottom of it. The score ranks poses, not activity, and this benchmark is why no claim on this part rests on a docking score alone.

**Figure 22 | Alanine scan of BoPEP4 against PEPR1.** Change in HADDOCK score relative to wild type for eighteen single-point alanine substitutions, Ser6 to Asn23, each built on the validated complex with the backbone held fixed and refined identically; positive values are destabilising. Bars are coloured as binding hotspots, structural or conformational signals, and neutral positions, with the ensemble mean marked on each. Eight positions clear +7, every one of them carried by a large electrostatic term. The scan returns −1.3 and −2.9 at S15A and G17A, the two substitutions published to cost roughly 100-fold and more than 4,000-fold in activity, which bounds what the method can be asked.
